title: ber- verbs
pattern: ber- + root: bekerja, bermain, berkeluarga · in speech: kerja, main
explanation: ber- makes a verb about what someone does or has, rather than something done to an object: berjalan (to walk), bekerja (to work), bermain (to play), berenang (to swim). On a noun it means having or using it: berkeluarga (to have a family), bersepeda (to ride a bike), berbahaya (dangerous, from bahaya, danger). In conversation it usually drops and you hear just the root: Kerja di mana? (Where do you work?), Main ke rumah, ya (Come over some time). It stays where the root alone means something else or isn't a verb: berangkat (to set off, while angkat is to lift), berhenti (to stop), berkeluarga. The spelling shrinks in a few words, so look up the root: berenang (renang), bekerja (kerja), belajar (ajar).
natural: In writing, on forms and when you want to sound careful: Saya bekerja di bank is a good answer to an official. In everyday polite conversation the short form is just as good: Saya kerja di bank.
stiff: Every ber- in a chat with friends sounds like a schoolbook: Mari kita berjalan-jalan is textbook, Jalan-jalan, yuk! is what people say. Don't drop it from a noun, though: Dia sudah berkeluarga, never Dia sudah keluarga.

gap.why: Before kerja, ber- loses its r: bekerja; mengerjakan is to work on something.
Having a family is ber- + keluarga, and the ber- stays even in speech, because keluarga alone is just the noun.
Setting off is berangkat, and the ber- stays, because angkat and mengangkat mean to lift.

examples.english: Come over to our place some time.

gap.note: Bermain ke rumah is correct too, but in a spoken invitation it sounds like a schoolbook.
gap.why: In speech the ber- drops: main ke rumah is the everyday way to say come over.
